title: Volta
summary: A sports-supplement online store you can click through end to end, with a made-up brand: catalogue, stack builder, a tiered club, a game that gives coupons, gifts and a panel for the owner. It all runs in the browser on sample data: it processes no payments and creates no real orders.

facts.v: 29 in the store · 60 in the panel
Demo: it charges and ships nothing

tldr.v: A small supplement shop takes orders over WhatsApp, chases price lists that keep changing, has tubs expiring on the shelf and doesn't know when each customer is about to run out.
A store that works out when to reorder, sells lots by expiry date and turns games into coupons, plus a panel where the owner sees what to do today.
A clickable demo with no backend, payments or customers. The production version is described in the repo, not built.

p: Volta is a demo to show a supplement shop owner how they could sell online. The brand, the sample city (Mar del Plata), the catalogue and the orders are made up.
list: Buyer: product sheets with price per serving, «how long will it last?», lot and expiry date; a search that knows the trade, a comparer, a stack builder, a quiz and a three-step checkout.
Club: levels by total spend, missions, a prize wheel and Shaker Rush, a canvas game that turns the score into a coupon.
Gifts: a code with a check digit and a link; whoever receives it never sees the price.

Owner: a panel with nine sections (Today, Counter, Orders, Stock, Purchasing, Customers, Promos, Campaigns and Settings), with lots that go out by expiry date and the supplier's price list imported from Excel.

p: The demo is built for a meeting with the owner, and its script opens with their pains. The core answer is reordering: getting the customer back before they buy somewhere else.
loop.title: The reorder loop

steps.d: The product sheet works out how long the tub lasts, and the customer can ask for a heads-up before it runs out.
From the variant's servings and the delivery date, the panel lists who runs out this week.
A ready-made WhatsApp message, with a link that loads the bag.
Opens the link with the bag ready; if they played in the Club, they have a coupon to use.

loop.loop: And the loop starts again. It is the concept the demo shows: there are no real customers or metrics to measure it.
loop.caption: Other ideas in the demo: 10 % off when three categories are combined (an editable rule), 17 dated campaigns with their coupon, and a brand sheet that turns it into another demo for another prospect.

p: A single Next.js app exported as a static site: there is no server and no database. Pages don't compute anything; they hand off to containers that join the state with a pure rules engine.

diagram.title: One app, all in the browser
diagram.caption: Published on GitHub Pages from CI. The only thing outside the browser is the server at the bottom: it is described in the repo and does not exist.

admin.label: Panel
admin.note: No login on purpose, with the «Demo» sign in view: it is not secure and is not presented as such.

engine.label: Pure engine
engine.note: Pricing, coupons, stock, order states and the game are pure, tested functions, with no React.

stores.label: Stores
stores.note: They rehydrate after the first render so the static HTML doesn't break, with versioned migrations of what was saved.

prod.label: Server
prod.note: In production the engine moves into server services and the components are reused. Described, not built.

orders.h: The order as a state machine
p: An order's life is what most needs to be right, so it lives in a single function that decides which transition is valid and with which trigger. The screen cannot skip a step.

diagram.title: From pending to delivered
diagram.caption: Every transition goes through canTransition. From payment on, each step is taken by someone in the panel, and the changes drop an email into a simulated outbox.

review.label: In review
review.note: A receipt never pays by itself: the panel approves it, or rejects it with a reason and the order goes back to pending.

paid.label: Paid
paid.note: It can also be reached directly when the payment provider confirms (a simulation) or the owner was paid in hand. In production that would be a signed webhook, with the server checking amount, currency and reference.

claim.label: In claim
claim.note: It opens from any paid state and ends in a return or goes back to the previous state.

security.h: Security: what is there and what isn't
p: A demo with no server can't be secure in the production sense, and it doesn't pretend to be. What it does is not ask for or send anything it shouldn't.

items.d: No secrets and no API: WhatsApp is a link with the text filled in, and a receipt photo is processed on a canvas in the browser. Nothing is uploaded.
Only the panel's approval or the provider's confirmation lead to Paid. The confirmation is simulated and says so on screen.
Zod with React Hook Form: lengths, emoji, phone and postcode. Files: only JPG, PNG or WebP.
Codes carry a check digit, and the link opens nothing if it is cut or edited.
Read-only across CI; writing to Pages only in the deploy step.
noindex and robots.txt, because it shows sample prices and brands.

items.t: Static export, no server at this stage
items.why: To publish it on GitHub Pages: the repo forbids in writing Server Actions, Route Handlers that read the request, cookies, middleware and ISR.
items.alt: A server from day one: left for production, described but not built.

items.t: Business rules in a pure engine
items.why: Pricing, stock, payments and missions live outside the components, so they are tested without a browser and can move to the server in production without rebuilding the screens.
Volta is a fork of an earlier store demo, which had already solved the hard, tested parts. Rebuilding them from scratch would have taken weeks.

items.t: White label through a brand sheet
items.why: One demo per prospect by changing a sheet: name, colours and its own storage prefix, so two demos on the same domain don't mix. A test forbids writing the brand name outside the sheets.
The static HTML doesn't know what the visitor saved: rehydrating afterwards avoids hydration errors. Saved state has versioned migrations.

items.t: A Canvas 2D game with a single loop
items.why: One requestAnimationFrame with a capped delta and the pixel ratio capped at 2. Whatever shows before hydration is CSS.

p: Strict TypeScript and ESLint. Before publishing, CI runs lint, typecheck, unit tests, the build, a check of the export and the e2e suite on an emulated phone.

items.d: Unit: pricing, orders, lots, reordering, game and brand
Playwright, listed in 93 files, not run

quality.note: I ran the unit tests with Vitest on 28/10/2026: 988 green, in 117 files. I listed the 893 e2e tests that day with Playwright's list mode, in 93 files; I didn't run them.

status.h: Status and what I don't claim
list: Demo. The brand, catalogue, customers and orders are fictional.
There is no backend, database, authentication, payments, real email or WhatsApp API. The production version is described in the repo, not built.
It has no customers or sales. I don't claim that reordering or gamification increase anything: there is no real data.
The duration and dosage calculators are indicative: they are not health advice.
Pending: splitting the panel's data from the store's, and testing on real iPhone and Android phones.
I listed the e2e tests, but didn't run them.
